blocks.prompt: The Cow Who Eats Twice
blocks.text: A cow eats grass fast. She does not chew it much. She swallows it in a big green lump. Later the cow lies down. She is done eating, but she is not done. Up comes the lump of grass, back into her mouth. Now she chews it slowly. This lump is called cud. Chewing it again is called chewing the cud. A cow chews her cud for about eight hours every day. Her jaw goes around and around. Grass is tough. Chewing it twice helps break it down.

blocks.prompt: The Four Rooms
blocks.text: Grass is one of the toughest foods on Earth. It is built out of a stiff material called cellulose, and that is what makes a blade of grass stand up straight instead of flopping over. Most animals cannot break cellulose down at all. A cow can, and her secret is her stomach. It is not one bag. It is four rooms in a row. The first room is called the rumen, and it is enormous. It can hold about as much as a bathtub. Grass goes in there and sits, warm and wet, while it softens. Then the cow does something odd. She brings a lump of that softened grass back up into her mouth and chews it all over again. The lump is called cud. She may chew her cud for eight hours a day, making as many as forty thousand jaw movements, grinding the grass finer and finer. The mash then moves on through the other three rooms. Each one takes out something the cow needs. By the end, tough grass has become milk and muscle and bone. A cow can spend half her life chewing, and she does it without any upper front teeth. She has a hard pad up there instead.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Rents Out Its Digestion
blocks.text: Here is a strange fact about cows. A cow cannot digest grass. Not one blade. No cow has ever produced the chemical needed to break down cellulose, the stiff material that makes a grass stem stand up straight. Neither can you, which is why a bowl of lawn clippings would leave you starving. So how does a cow live on a field of the stuff? She does not digest her food. She rents out the job. Inside the rumen, the first and largest chamber of her stomach, live billions upon billions of microbes: bacteria, fungi, and single celled creatures far too small to see. A single teaspoon of rumen fluid can hold more of them than there are people on Earth. The cow supplies them with a warm, wet, airless tank and a steady delivery of chopped grass. They supply her with the one thing she lacks, the enzyme that cuts cellulose apart. The microbes eat the grass. As they feed, they release simple acids into the fluid around them, and the cow absorbs those acids straight through the wall of her rumen. Those acids, not the grass, are her actual food. She is not living on the meadow. She is living on what her tenants leave behind. Then comes the part that seems unfair. The mash flows out of the rumen into the later chambers, where the cow digests the microbes themselves. They are where most of her protein comes from. She grows them, harvests them, and eats them, over and over, for her whole life.

notes: Every cow descends from a wild animal called the aurochs

blocks.prompt: Eighty Animals Became a Billion
blocks.text: Walk past a field and you will see an animal so ordinary it is almost invisible. There are roughly one and a half billion cattle alive right now, on every continent except Antarctica. It is easy to assume they have always been there, standing around, waiting for us. They have not. Every cow on Earth descends from a wild animal called the aurochs. An aurochs bull stood nearly six feet at the shoulder, carried horns that swept forward like a dare, and was fierce enough that Roman writers treated hunting one as a test of nerve. Around ten thousand five hundred years ago, in the hills of the Near East, people began keeping them instead of hunting them. Genetic studies suggest that the entire taurine cattle line traces back to a founding group of only about eighty wild females. Eighty animals became a billion and a half. The aurochs itself did not survive the arrangement. Forests were cleared, herds were hunted, and the last known aurochs died in 1627, in the Jaktorow Forest in Poland. The wild original is gone. Its tame descendants are everywhere. What made cattle worth keeping was not their size alone. It was a trick they had perfected long before people arrived: turning grass into food. Grass grows on land that will not grow wheat. It survives drought, frost, and grazing, and it comes back. But grass is armored in cellulose, and no mammal can break cellulose down. The cow gets around that by carrying a fermentation tank inside her body. Her rumen holds about fifty gallons of warm fluid packed with microbes that can cut cellulose apart. They digest the grass, she absorbs the acids they release, and later she digests the microbes themselves. That is the real bargain. A cow converts a landscape people cannot eat into milk, meat, leather, and pulling power. For most of history she was also the tractor. Some human populations changed in response: the ability to drink milk as an adult spread through herding peoples, because those who could do it got through hungry years better than those who could not. We did not simply tame the cow. Over ten thousand years we reshaped her, and she reshaped us.

6.title: The Cow That Cannot Digest Grass
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Cow That Cannot Digest Grass

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Bos taurus, descended from the wild aurochs
The rumen: a 50 gallon fermentation vat kept at body heat
Microbes make the enzyme; the cow never has
She lives on their waste acids, then digests them
Methanogens in the rumen make methane, released by belching
About 1.5 billion cattle alive, all of it our doing

blocks.prompt: The Borrowed Stomach
blocks.text: Consider what a cow is actually doing when she stands in a field, apparently doing nothing. She is eating grass, which sounds unremarkable until you look at grass closely. A blade of grass stands upright because its cells are wrapped in cellulose, a molecule built from sugar rings locked together in a chain so stable that it works as structural material. Wood is mostly cellulose. Cotton is nearly pure cellulose. Paper is cellulose. It is one of the most abundant substances on the planet, it is packed with energy, and almost nothing with a backbone can open it. The cow certainly cannot. No cow has ever produced the enzyme that cuts a cellulose chain, and neither have you. To a vertebrate, a meadow is a locked pantry. The cow solves this by not solving it. She subcontracts. The first chamber of her four part stomach, the rumen, is a fifty gallon fermentation vat held at body heat with the oxygen kept out, and it is not empty. It teems. A single drop of rumen fluid holds billions of bacteria, along with fungi, protozoa, and archaea. Those organisms do own the enzyme. The cow provides the tank, the warmth, the constant stirring, and the raw material. Her tenants provide the chemistry. Then the arrangement gets stranger. As the microbes ferment cellulose, they release short carbon chains called volatile fatty acids, and the cow absorbs them directly through the rumen wall. Those acids supply most of her energy. She is not fueled by grass. She is fueled by microbial waste. And when the fermented mash finally moves into her later chambers, she digests the microbes themselves, which is where most of her protein comes from. She grows them, then eats them. A cow is less an animal that eats plants than a farmer running the same farm inside herself. The cud is part of the machinery. Grass swallowed quickly comes back up in lumps to be reground, up to forty thousand jaw movements a day, because microbes work on surface area and chewing creates more of it. A cow may spend eight hours a day at it. She does this without upper front teeth, using a hard pad instead, and it is enough. There is a cost, and it is why cattle turn up in climate reports. Fermentation without oxygen produces methane. The archaea in the rumen make it, and the cow disposes of it by belching, roughly once a minute, all day long. Methane traps far more heat in the atmosphere than the same weight of carbon dioxide does over the twenty years after it is released. With around one and a half billion cattle alive, that belching adds up to one of the largest single sources of methane on Earth. Here is the part worth sitting with. One and a half billion is not a natural number. Cattle descend from the aurochs, a wild animal domesticated in the Near East roughly ten thousand five hundred years ago and hunted out of existence by 1627. Every cow alive is the result of a decision people made, and repeated for four hundred generations, to keep the animals that turned useless land into milk. The rumen is ancient. The scale is ours.
